record.title: CLR-Bench tests whether self-evolving agents infer hidden rules from feedback
record.summary: The 29 October arXiv preprint introduces CLR-Bench, a benchmark of 20 four-level curriculum chains across 10 constructed domains. It tests whether six self-evolution methods infer hidden named groupings from sparse feedback and transfer them to unseen values, rather than retaining corrections as exceptions. The authors report weak feedback-only generalization for GPT-6-Luna, improvement with a fixed lesson, and substantially stronger results for selected methods with GPT-6-Sol. These are author-reported results on a small constructed benchmark; they do not establish general agent learning or operational transfer.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The paper and linked public repository describe and provide 20 four-level chains across 10 domains, with 80 hidden rules, practice tasks and test tasks; the benchmark uses probe-certified hidden groupings and diagnostics for missed members and false exclusions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On the authors’ benchmark, six self-evolution methods show limited feedback-only generalization with GPT-6-Luna; a fixed named-grouping lesson raises some methods’ scores, while ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet score higher with GPT-6-Sol. Outcomes vary by model and update method.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The study does not establish that benchmark results predict learning from feedback in open-ended, real-world agent deployments, and its reported comparisons have not been independently reproduced.

evidence_gaps.description: The reported model and update-method comparisons have not been independently reproduced on CLR-Bench or broader task distributions.

brief.importance_rationale: If adopted, a benchmark that distinguishes rule induction from exception memorization could change evaluation choices for persistent-state agents. Its current consequence is bounded by 20 constructed chains, two evaluated base models and no established independent use.
limitations: The benchmark has 20 constructed chains in 10 domains, with only two chains per domain.
The paper reports each condition over the benchmark’s 20 chains; no independent reproduction or external evaluation was found in this review.

The results depend on the evaluated models, prompts/update methods and benchmark convention that hidden labels denote named groupings; they do not directly establish performance on open-ended real-world feedback.
The linked repository is publicly visible, but its license is listed as undecided; no code or data was executed or adopted here.
brief.summary: The 29 October arXiv preprint introduces CLR-Bench, a benchmark of 20 four-level curriculum chains across 10 constructed domains. It tests whether six self-evolution methods infer hidden named groupings from sparse feedback and transfer them to unseen values, rather than retaining corrections as exceptions. The authors report weak feedback-only generalization for GPT-6-Luna, improvement with a fixed lesson, and substantially stronger results for selected methods with GPT-6-Sol. These are author-reported results on a small constructed benchmark; they do not establish general agent learning or operational transfer.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report that methods with GPT-6-Luna generally store corrections as exceptions and gain at most about five points over the frozen baseline; a fixed lesson improves several results. ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet perform substantially better with GPT-6-Sol. Results depend strongly on base model and update method.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accessible paper documents the benchmark design and the public repository contains benchmark data, scoring and harness components. Their presence does not independently validate the reported scores; no execution or reproduction was performed.
technical.mechanism: Each chain adds a hidden named-grouping rule to a persistent task. Practice feedback reveals a member and a non-member; separate test tasks measure whether the agent applies the grouping to unseen members while retaining non-members. The authors use probes to check prior knowledge and identifiability, then score under- and over-generalization separately.
technical.novelty: Tests what persistent-state agents learned by checking transfer to unseen members of hidden named groupings, rather than relying on aggregate score gains alone.
technical.regime: 20 four-level chains across 10 constructed domains; six self-evolution methods; GPT-6-Luna and selected GPT-6-Sol conditions at high reasoning effort; 80 hidden rules with distinct practice and test tasks.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links code and data; the repository documents local scoring and model-dependent runs. The repository lists its license as undecided. No code was executed and no independent reproduction was done.
technical.strongest_baseline: Frozen agent, raw practice-history reference, and fixed-lesson condition on the same 20 chains; comparisons are author-reported and run once per condition per chain.

brief.title: CLR-Bench tests whether self-evolving agents infer hidden rules from feedback
brief.why_it_matters: Persistent agent state is often expected to turn feedback into reusable knowledge. CLR-Bench isolates a particular failure mode—storing individual corrections instead of inferring a rule—and separates it from over-generalization using value-level diagnostics. If the benchmark proves useful beyond its initial tasks, it could improve how self-evolving agents are evaluated; the current results remain narrow and unreplicated.
